bull_bear.body: Confident on structural long-term trends (4WD shift, export hub status) but prudently cautious on near-term FY27 guidance due to macro/geopolitical volatility; Emphasized execution discipline and 'watchtower' monitoring of costs.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: Management explicitly linked the 4WD surge to GST reduction narrowing the price gap with 2WD, creating a permanent structural shift rather than cyclical bump; Q4 margin dip in specific axle categories was a strategic choice to prioritize customer supply continuity over immediate cost efficiency, absorbing fixed costs better overall.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Balance sheet de-levering: debt to equity declined from 0.62x at Mar-22 to 0.27x at Mar-26.
- Return ratios shown improving over FY22-FY26: ROCE from 10.0% to 29.2% and ROE from 7.9% to 25.5%.
- Working capital discipline: net working capital days of 0, 15, 28, 45 and 38 over FY22-FY26, with inventory days 77/73/80/83/70, debtor days 63/65/50/59/61 and creditor days 140/123/102/97/93.
- Cash generation funds reinvestment: net cash from operating activities of INR 1,558 Mn in FY26 against net cash used in investing of INR 337 Mn and in financing of INR 939 Mn.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer concentration — A large part of revenue comes from a few OEM customers; if any cuts orders, shifts to in-house production or moves to a competitor, volumes and plant utilisation are significantly affected. Mitigated by widening the customer base, an updated product portfolio and long-term supply agreements (LTAs).
- Group dependency — Reliance on Carraro Group entities for technology and procurement could limit operational independence. Mitigated by building design and testing capability in India, developing local suppliers for critical parts and formal agreements with the Group on technology support and supply continuity.
- Related party transaction intensity — A high volume of intercompany transactions with Group entities may raise governance and compliance concerns; managed through Audit Committee review, periodic transfer-pricing benchmarking and disclosure aligned with the Companies Act and SEBI LODR.
- Seasonality and cyclicality of end markets — Demand is linked to the farming season and to construction and commercial vehicle cycles, causing revenue and plant workload to swing sharply quarter to quarter; balanced through segment mix and flexible manpower arrangements.
- Industry and technology transition (electrification) — The pace of OEM investment in electrification and hybridisation is uncertain, and continued reliance on conventional mechanical drivelines risks share loss if customers transition faster than the Company's e-axle and hybrid offering matures; mitigated by co-developing e-axle and hybrid platforms with Group R&D and phasing capex to confirmed programme awards.
- Raw material cost volatility and margin pressure — Steel, alloy and other input costs remain volatile while OEM price negotiations lag cost movements, compressing realised margins; addressed through indexed pricing clauses where feasible, efficiency and cost-reduction projects.
- Geopolitical and supply chain disruption — Shipping-route disruption, tariff actions and concentrated sourcing for certain components expose input costs and delivery schedules to events outside the Company's control; mitigated by dual-sourcing of critical items, strategic buffer stock and scenario-based monitoring of freight and landed costs.
- Cybersecurity and data privacy — Increasing use of technology raises exposure to cyber-attacks, while DPDPA obligations add compliance burden around personal data handling; addressed through an updated IT security framework implemented across group entities and third-party consultant support for DPDPA compliance.
- Internal market overlap with related entities — Competitive dynamics within the broader industry and potential overlaps with related Carraro entities may impact market positioning; managed through geographical segmentation, market-specific strategies and enhancing business independence via purchase of intellectual property rights.
- Energy intensity of manufacturing — Heat treatment of gears and shafts is the most energy-intensive stage of driveline manufacturing, so energy costs are a significant portion of operating expenditure, and dependence on non-renewable fuels such as PNG and diesel exposes the Company to energy price volatility, carbon-related regulation and customer emissions scrutiny (BRSR material issues table).

business.body: Carraro India Limited, a subsidiary of the Italy-based Carraro Group, designs, manufactures and supplies axles, transmission systems, gears and related driveline components for off-highway vehicles - agricultural tractors and construction vehicles such as backhoe loaders, telescopic boom handlers, soil compactors, cranes, self-loading concrete mixers and small motor graders. Its customers are OEMs, primarily India-based (including international OEMs with Indian operations), with exports routed largely through holding company Carraro SpA; the Company describes itself as a technology-driven integrated supplier whose products are critical components of its customers' final products. Alongside manufacturing it sells engineering services to external customers, drawing on its Ranjangaon R&D centre and its R&D subsidiary Carraro Technologies India Private Limited, and supplies spare parts and aftermarket support.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Five strategic priorities anchored in resilience, trust and future readiness - reading industry direction early, deepening customer partnerships and investing in next-generation technologies across the agricultural and construction equipment markets.
- Ride the structural shift to 4WD and higher-horsepower tractors, where advanced axle and transmission demand sits squarely in the Company's core strengths.
- Deepen localisation of raw materials and components, progressing towards a medium-term localisation target of 86-88% (78.1% in 2025-26, up from 77.0%), to improve supply security, shorten lead times and strengthen cost competitiveness.
- Operate a dual-sourcing strategy with a minimum of two suppliers per component across a 247-supplier base (177 domestic), build long-term supplier partnerships through capability-building programmes and technical workshops, and selectively integrate critical components vertically.
- Defend the driveline moat through deep application expertise, integrated OEM co-engineering and high switching costs backed by long validation cycles and deeply embedded product architecture.
- Build future-ready platforms for electrification: develop electric and hydrostatic-electric drivelines, pursue joint technology development with the Carraro Group across electric, hybrid and advanced transmission platforms, provide engineering services for e-transmission industrialisation, develop CVT technology for future tractor applications and invest continually in EV transmission design, validation and specialised engineering skills.
- Scale engineering services into a standalone growth engine - about `100 Million generated during 2025-26, with a new agreement with Montra Electric to industrialise and supply e-transmissions.
- Invest ahead of demand in manufacturing capacity: `417 Million deployed in 2025-26 across telescopic handler axle programmes, advanced transmission platforms and additional capacity, with the Board approving a programme to further increase annual axle production capacity from 2026-27.
- Broaden customer reach and supply-chain strength - first authorised service centre opened at Faridabad, plus deeper localisation and supplier development.
- Sustain innovation throughput from the in-house R&D centre and the Group's global engineering network (Italy, China, Luxembourg): 16 prototypes developed during the year and four taken into production, focused on higher-horsepower drivelines and advanced transmission technologies.
- Continue evolving from a manufacturing-focused organisation into an integrated engineering and technology-driven enterprise, strengthened by the integration of Carraro Technologies India Private Limited and its Pune engineering centre.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Carraro India is expanding ahead of demand at its Ranjangaon, Pune site. To support expected demand growth across both agricultural and construction equipment applications, the Board approved a capital expenditure programme of approximately `623 Million to expand axle manufacturing capacity from about 134,028 units to about 154,160 units over the next 18 months. During 2025-26 the Company incurred capital expenditure of approximately `417 Million on telescopic handler (TBH) axle production, a new high-performance transmission range for agricultural applications, and incremental capacity for 2025-26 sales; the Board's newly approved programme is a further, separate step and the Chairman's message describes a new phase of investments and capacity expansion starting in 2026-27. At the driveline plant (Plant 1) the expansion is phased: Phase 1 covers a paint shop and finished-goods warehouse, Phase 2 a new assembly line and incoming-material warehouse, and Phase 3 a new administrative building, alongside the additional approved axle capacity. Manufacturing upgrades during the year included sealed-quench furnaces and a Mazak machining centre. Other capability additions in the period were the inauguration of the Company's first authorised service centre at Faridabad and continued investment in localisation, automation and process improvement; the pipeline the capacity is being built for is the 4WD axle ramp, the TBH axle programme for an international OEM, higher-horsepower transmission programmes and a bull-gear nomination starting 2027-28.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Structural 2WD-to-4WD tractor shift: in 2025-26, 23%-25% of the tractor market above 40 HP shifted from 2WD to 4WD, with 4WD tractor volumes expected to grow at a CAGR of 19.1%, well ahead of conventional tractor segments.
- India contributes nearly 35-40% of global tractor demand, and growing preference for higher-horsepower tractors is increasing demand for advanced transmission systems and axle solutions.
- Adoption of TREM IV/V norms is expected to support premiumisation and export opportunities.
- Domestic tractor industry recorded its best-ever annual volumes in 2025-26 with wholesale sales crossing the 10 Lakh unit milestone; total tractor sales including exports reached approximately 12.6 Lakh units and production exceeded 11.5 Lakh units.
- Long-term tractor outlook remains favourable on rising mechanisation, government support (SMAM, Custom Hiring Centres), higher rural incomes, improved credit access through the KCC ecosystem and rising labour costs pushing mechanisation.
- Construction equipment is a two-sided story: domestic sales fell approximately 2% year-on-year to 136,995 units on slower project execution and delayed awards (ICEMA data cited in the Board's Report shows a ~7% decline to 1,13,229 units), while exports rose nearly 32% on demand from African, Middle Eastern and Latin American markets.
- Infrastructure-led demand anchors the medium term: PM GatiShakti, the National Infrastructure Pipeline (over USD 1.4 Trillion), Bharatmala, PMAY, Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0, PMGSY and a `2.93 Lakh Crore railway capital outlay in the Union Budget 2026-27.
- Export competitiveness and deepening localisation (more than 95% of construction equipment sold domestically is now made in India) are the supply-side gains expected to carry India towards being the second-largest construction equipment market by 2030.
- Margin levers stated by management: operating leverage on higher volumes, disciplined cost management, continued localisation gains and a richer product mix with greater contribution from high-value 4WD axles and TBH programmes.
- Mix shift towards exports: export sales contributed 36% of total revenue, up from 32.8% in the prior year, led by TBH axles for a global OEM and recovering demand for tractor axles in international markets.
- Market position underpinning the demand narrative: 60%+ share of non-captive 4WD tractor axles (>40 HP), 100% of non-captive AG tractor transmissions (>40 HP) and 60%+ of non-captive construction vehicle transmissions.
- Off-highway industry structural shifts - tightening emission norms, fuel-efficiency and technology preferences, and the early-stage emergence of electrification in agricultural tractors - are pushing OEMs to invest in engineering and electrification roadmaps, widening the Company's engineering services opportunity.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Carraro India delivered a beat-and-raise FY26 with 25% revenue growth and 60bps margin expansion to 10.8%, driven by the structural GST-induced shift to 4WD tractors and robust construction exports. While FY27 guidance is cautiously tempered to 4-8% due to geopolitical volatility, the medium-term trajectory remains intact with a raised FY30 revenue target of INR 3,500-4,000 crores and deepening localization (78% to ~88%) supporting profitability.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Structural 2WD-to-4WD tractor shift: in 2025-26, 23%-25% of the tractor market above 40 HP shifted from 2WD to 4WD, with 4WD tractor volumes expected to grow at a CAGR of 19.1%, well ahead of conventional tractor segments.
- India contributes nearly 35-40% of global tractor demand, and growing preference for higher-horsepower tractors is increasing demand for advanced transmission systems and axle solutions.
- Adoption of TREM IV/V norms is expected to support premiumisation and export opportunities.
- Domestic tractor industry recorded its best-ever annual volumes in 2025-26 with wholesale sales crossing the 10 Lakh unit milestone; total tractor sales including exports reached approximately 12.6 Lakh units and production exceeded 11.5 Lakh units.
- Long-term tractor outlook remains favourable on rising mechanisation, government support (SMAM, Custom Hiring Centres), higher rural incomes, improved credit access through the KCC ecosystem and rising labour costs pushing mechanisation.
- Construction equipment is a two-sided story: domestic sales fell approximately 2% year-on-year to 136,995 units on slower project execution and delayed awards (ICEMA data cited in the Board's Report shows a ~7% decline to 1,13,229 units), while exports rose nearly 32% on demand from African, Middle Eastern and Latin American markets.
- Infrastructure-led demand anchors the medium term: PM GatiShakti, the National Infrastructure Pipeline (over USD 1.4 Trillion), Bharatmala, PMAY, Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT 2.0, PMGSY and a `2.93 Lakh Crore railway capital outlay in the Union Budget 2026-27.
- Export competitiveness and deepening localisation (more than 95% of construction equipment sold domestically is now made in India) are the supply-side gains expected to carry India towards being the second-largest construction equipment market by 2030.
- Margin levers stated by management: operating leverage on higher volumes, disciplined cost management, continued localisation gains and a richer product mix with greater contribution from high-value 4WD axles and TBH programmes.
- Mix shift towards exports: export sales contributed 36% of total revenue, up from 32.8% in the prior year, led by TBH axles for a global OEM and recovering demand for tractor axles in international markets.
- Market position underpinning the demand narrative: 60%+ share of non-captive 4WD tractor axles (>40 HP), 100% of non-captive AG tractor transmissions (>40 HP) and 60%+ of non-captive construction vehicle transmissions.
- Off-highway industry structural shifts - tightening emission norms, fuel-efficiency and technology preferences, and the early-stage emergence of electrification in agricultural tractors - are pushing OEMs to invest in engineering and electrification roadmaps, widening the Company's engineering services opportunity.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: FY26 Margin 10.8% driven by operating leverage, product mix (4WD), and localization (78% RM localized). Q4 RM % increase attributed to adverse product mix (rush dispatches) rather than commodity inflation. Pass-through mechanism typically lags 3 months. Labor availability cited as emerging cost pressure.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Dividend: INR 6.75/share (Final), ~30% payout ratio. Balance sheet strengthening prioritized (D/E 0.27x). Reinvestment in capacity and technology for FY30 growth targets.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Carraro India is expanding ahead of demand at its Ranjangaon, Pune site. To support expected demand growth across both agricultural and construction equipment applications, the Board approved a capital expenditure programme of approximately `623 Million to expand axle manufacturing capacity from about 134,028 units to about 154,160 units over the next 18 months. During 2025-26 the Company incurred capital expenditure of approximately `417 Million on telescopic handler (TBH) axle production, a new high-performance transmission range for agricultural applications, and incremental capacity for 2025-26 sales; the Board's newly approved programme is a further, separate step and the Chairman's message describes a new phase of investments and capacity expansion starting in 2026-27. At the driveline plant (Plant 1) the expansion is phased: Phase 1 covers a paint shop and finished-goods warehouse, Phase 2 a new assembly line and incoming-material warehouse, and Phase 3 a new administrative building, alongside the additional approved axle capacity. Manufacturing upgrades during the year included sealed-quench furnaces and a Mazak machining centre. Other capability additions in the period were the inauguration of the Company's first authorised service centre at Faridabad and continued investment in localisation, automation and process improvement; the pipeline the capacity is being built for is the 4WD axle ramp, the TBH axle programme for an international OEM, higher-horsepower transmission programmes and a bull-gear nomination starting 2027-28.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident on structural long-term trends (4WD shift, export hub status) but prudently cautious on near-term FY27 guidance due to macro/geopolitical volatility; Emphasized execution discipline and 'watchtower' monitoring of costs.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Designated global centre of excellence for agricultural transmissions within the Carraro Group and one of the Group's largest manufacturing locations, positioning it for future product programmes, technology transfers and global sourcing
- Long-lived OEM relationships: the top 10 customers by revenue contribution have engaged the Company continuously for at least 15 years, and six new customers were onboarded during the year
- Products are critical components of customers' final products, giving high embeddedness in OEM platforms
- Strong position in the domestic non-captive 4WD axle market, deepened during the year in higher-value transmission applications
- Engineering depth: in-house R&D centre plus R&D subsidiary Carraro Technologies India Private Limited, connected to Group engineering hubs in Italy, China and Luxembourg; engineering services revenue reached about `100 Million in 2025-26
- Vertically integrated manufacturing at one site - cast machining, heat treatment, gear manufacturing, assembly, painting, prototyping and testing across an 84,000 sq. m. driveline plant and a 78,000 sq. m. gear plant
- Deepening localisation of raw materials and components, supporting supply-chain resilience and cost optimisation
- Early positioning in off-highway electrification through the Montra Electric e-transmission engineering services agreement and CVT / higher-horsepower platform development

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Geopolitical tension in West Asia impacting energy prices/supply chain (H1 FY27 risk); Monsoon uncertainty affecting rural demand; Global tariff volatility (US/Europe); Labor availability constraints; Raw material price fluctuations.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Management explicitly linked the 4WD surge to GST reduction narrowing the price gap with 2WD, creating a permanent structural shift rather than cyclical bump; Q4 margin dip in specific axle categories was a strategic choice to prioritize customer supply continuity over immediate cost efficiency, absorbing fixed costs better overall.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:

themes.title: Auto OEM cycle - CV replacement & PV premiumization
themes.need: GST 2.0 rate rationalization plus an aged CV fleet still frames the replacement cycle, but Q1FY27's real signal is 2W OEMs EXPANDING margin through a commodity shock. TVSMOTOR sold 1.63mn units (+28%) on INR 13,896cr revenue (+38%) while lifting EBITDA margin 30bps to 12.8% having absorbed a ~4% commodity shock with only ~1.5% of price increase (CARE upgraded it AA+ to AAA), and committed 2W capacity from 6.8mn to 8.3mn by Q4FY27. BAJAJ-AUTO set volume/revenue/EBITDA records with margin at 20.9% (+110bps) through ~4.5% commodity inflation AND ~10% of volume lost to a ransomware shutdown, with EV now 30% of domestic revenue at double-digit EBITDA and Chetak EBITDA-positive - a scaled, profitable EV second engine. Commercial mobility is electrifying fastest: TVSMOTOR's 3W EV penetration crossed 40% for the first time. ASHOKLEY's all-time-high CV volumes (220k units, MHCV share 30.8%) carry the CV leg with defence + Switch EV optionality; TMCV/TMPV/SMLMAH/ESCORTS on CV/tractors; APOLLOTYRE/JKTYRE/BALKRISIND/MRF on tyres.
themes.driver: Capacity commissioning against demand (TVSMOTOR 2W to 8.3mn by Q4FY27, BAJAJ-AUTO 7m to 9m+ units); 3W/2W EV penetration inflection; GST-2.0 price-cut demand, aged-fleet replacement and festive 2W/PV.
